Opinion Newsmaker of the Week

Old guard, new blood and a fight for the soul of the Democratic Party

From Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries to James Talarico and Zohran Mamdani, the US midterm election has exposed competing visions of what the Democratic Party should stand for and who should lead it.

Debdutta Chakraborty

07 November, 2026 08:15 am IST

T he Democrats have won back political power in the US after a long drought, but the blue tsunami, as the 2026 midterm election results are being labelled, has reopened a more contentious question: who owns the party now—the established leadership that has steered it for decades, or a new generation that wants to change its politics, priorities and relationship with voters?

Tuesday’s victories cut across the Democratic Party’s ideological spectrum, producing wins for the old guard as well as political outsiders. Progressives scored breakthrough victories in Senate races in Michigan and Maine, alongside gains in the House of Representatives. More moderate Democrats, meanwhile, pulled off stunning upsets in Republican strongholds such as Kansas and South Carolina, while flipping North Carolina and holding on to Georgia.

While the Republican rout in the midterms has given Democrats a new majority and fresh political momentum, beneath the victory laps lies a contest between an old guard under pressure, a progressive generation demanding change and a party still searching for the leader and ideas that can carry it into 2028.

Show Full Article

The Democratic sweep in Congress is ThePrint Newsmaker of the Week, not simply because it has changed the balance of power in Washington, but because it has reopened a contest over the meaning of the Democratic Party and exposed a war over its soul.

Also read: From Zohran Mamdani to Abdul El-Sayed—US voters are challenging Trump’s identity politics

The old guns vs new blood House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries and Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer have both secured the majorities they sought. Yet their victories come with a difficult balancing act: leading ideologically diverse caucuses that include lawmakers who campaigned against their own leadership.

For Schumer, the contest for power has already become personal. The 75-year-old New York senator has expressed confidence that he will be re-elected to lead the party’s enlarged Senate caucus.

But seven incoming senators are unwilling to offer him their support. They include Illinois Senator-elect Juliana Stratton and Kansas Senator-elect Adam Hamilton. Maine Senator-elect Troy Jackson said he had told Schumer he would “support somebody else”, while Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed has said he will support Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen for the post.

Minnesota Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan was more direct: “It is time for new leadership.” New Hampshire Senator-elect Chris Pappas said voters were hungry for “a new generation of leadership in the Senate”. Texas Senator-elect James Talarico has called for “new blood” in Washington.

The rebellion is not merely about age. It reflects broader dissatisfaction with how the party has responded to Trump and the compromises its leadership has been willing to make.

Schumer has also become a focal point for the party’s divisions over Israel. The first Jewish leader of the Senate, he has repeatedly described support for Israel as a central responsibility.

The same issue confronts Jeffries. He is staunchly anti-Trump but avowedly pro-Israel. Once the new Congress convenes in January, the 56-year-old is likely to become the first African American to hold the post of Speaker of the House. But, labelled “one of the most pro-Israel Democrats in the House”, Jeffries will have to manage a narrow and ideologically diverse Democratic majority, navigate divisions over Israel and work with progressives who have questioned whether his cautious, consensus-driven leadership suits the moment.

For some Democrats, that commitment is increasingly difficult to reconcile with the views of voters and activists who have demanded a reassessment of American support for Israel, particularly during the war in Gaza. The disagreement is about more than foreign policy. It has become a test of whether the party’s established alliances can survive a changing electorate and whether its leadership is prepared to accommodate a generation less willing to treat those alliances as beyond question.

Also read: The republic against its president

The politics of a new generation The election has produced no obvious heir to the party’s established leadership and no clear presidential front-runner for 2028. Gavin Newsom, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Kamala Harris remain among the names being discussed as possible contenders. But the results have brought a different set of politicians into the national conversation.

In Texas, James Talarico’s victory was particularly significant. At 37, the Presbyterian minister-in-training defeated Trump-backed Ken Paxton by 12 percentage points. Texas had not elected a Democrat to the Senate in 38 years, and Trump had carried the state comfortably in the 2024 presidential election.

His campaign offered an alternative to the familiar language of partisan combat. Talarico spoke frequently about Christianity and liberal values, drew on his experience working with Republicans in the Texas legislature and framed the political divide as one between the powerful and ordinary people. He rejected the idea of a “blue wave”, preferring to emphasise the breadth of the coalition he was trying to assemble. He also kept prominent national Democrats at a distance, running, in part, against the party establishment.

In Georgia, 39-year-old Jon Ossoff won re-election against Republican Mike Collins, using a campaign that extended beyond conventional television appearances. On Stephen Colbert’s now-defunct late-night programme, he discussed what he called “The Epstein Class” — wealthy and politically connected people who, he argues, behave as if ordinary rules do not apply to them.

Ossoff has previously ruled out a presidential run in 2028, saying he has “no interest” in seeking the office. Yet his growing national profile has made him a figure to watch. A Race to the White House polling average placed him fifth among potential Democratic nominees, while Polymarket put him first in its market for the party’s nomination. These figures are not a forecast, but they suggest how quickly a successful Senate campaign can become part of a national political conversation.

Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed, however, represents a different strand of the emerging Democratic coalition. His victory over Republican Mike Rogers made him the first Muslim senator in US history. During the campaign, Trump repeatedly attacked him, baselessly associating him with the Muslim Brotherhood and ridiculing his name. El-Sayed responded in his victory speech: “Donald, look, I know you struggled with my name, so after JD [Vance] swears me in in January, you could just go on and call me ‘Senator’.”

His campaign was also marked by a rupture within his own party. Haley Stevens, whom he had defeated in the Democratic primary, endorsed Rogers shortly before Election Day. El-Sayed nevertheless won Michigan by seven points, running on a progressive, anti-establishment platform that included criticism of American involvement in West Asia and support for Israel.

The careers of Talarico, Ossoff and El-Sayed do not point to a single new Democratic formula. One has made faith and political reconciliation central to his message; another has built a national profile through digital campaigning and criticism of concentrated wealth; the third has challenged the party’s orthodoxy. Their differences may be as important as their shared generational appeal.

Also read: The new American Left faces an old challenge – turning ideals into reality

Idological tensions and political temperaments The ideological disagreement is older than this election. Democrats have long been divided between pragmatists, who argue that the party must move towards the centre to win, and progressives, who believe it must offer voters a more ambitious alternative. The midterms have not resolved the dispute. They have given both sides reasons to believe they were right.

The progressive wing sees an opening for policies such as higher taxes on the wealthiest Americans and universal healthcare. Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez helped build momentum through their “Fighting Oligarchy” rallies in 2025, which focused on inequality and the political influence of wealthy interests. During the campaign season, Democrats also placed greater emphasis on the cost of living and economic insecurity.

Beyond the two major parties, the elections have highlighted the growing influence of another political force that could reshape the American political landscape: the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), the country’s largest socialist organisation. It does not operate as a separate electoral party but works as a left-wing organisation within the Democratic Party, seeking to push its politics and policy agenda further to the left. Its prominent figures include AOC, Rashida Tlaib, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Nithya Raman, who won the mayoral election in Los Angeles on Friday.

But there is also a more cautious Democratic view. A rejection of Trump does not automatically translate into an endorsement of every proposal from the Democratic left.

American political scientist Michael Parenti once called the Democrats “lily-livered, weasel-assed collaborators”. But modern-day socialist Democrat Zohran Mamdani offered a different vision when he said: “We will leave mediocrity in our past. No longer will we have to open a history book for proof that Democrats can dare to be great.”

Between these two quotes and their contentions, the Democrats’ midterm triumph looks less like a crowning moment than an episode of Succession : everyone wants the inheritance, but no one agrees on who should run the family business.

With Trump now a lame duck, the next two years will reveal whether the Democrats can turn an anti-Trump coalition into a governing one. They will have to decide how to confront the administration, address healthcare and the cost of living, where to stand on immigration and Israel, and how much authority to give a generation that won elections by questioning the party’s old habits.

Views are personal.

(Edited by Prashant Dixit)

Nov 7 (Reuters) – Russian forces launched a missile attack on the Ukrainian capital Kyiv early on Saturday, with debris damaging a residential building, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.

“Explosions in the Kyiv suburbs. The enemy is hitting infrastructure with ballistic missiles,” Klitschko wrote on Telegram.

Klitschko said debris had struck a five-storey apartment building in a western district of the capital. The facade of another residential building was also damaged.

Show Full Article

The city’s military administration, also writing on Telegram, said two people were injured and a building housing a kindergarten was damaged.

Officials continued to warn residents of the potential for more strikes hours after the attack.

President Volodymyr Zelenskiy had earlier said in his nightly video address that Russia was preparing new attacks on energy targets, bridges and other infrastructure.

The attacks occurred three days before US-led talks including Ukrainian and Russian negotiators were to open in Abu Dhabi seeking a resolution to the 4-1/2-year-old war. The last such talks took place in February.

(Reporting by Gleb Garanich, Writing by Ron Popeski; Editing by Cynthia Osterman)

By Bo Erickson, Nandita Bose, Steve Holland and Trevor Hunnicutt WASHINGTON, Nov 6 (Reuters) – US President Donald Trump named longtime aide Stephen Miller as his chief of staff on Friday, giving the architect of some of his toughest domestic policies one of the most powerful jobs in Washington after Republicans lost control of Congress.

Miller, who will replace Susie Wiles, assumes the role as the president prepares to confront a Democratic-led House of Representatives and Senate and a wave of congressional investigations into his administration.

A longtime proponent of expansive presidential authority, Miller takes over at a moment when the Republican Party’s defeat in Tuesday’s midterm elections could leave Trump more reliant on executive power to advance his domestic agenda.

Show Full Article

In a social media post, Trump called Miller “one of my most trusted advisors,” and praised Wiles for doing “an outstanding job.” Trump said the change would take effect on Monday.

A White House official said Miller’s appointment signals that Trump has no intention of rethinking his policies and instead is rewarding his most loyal aides.

“He’s not changing course,” the official said, despite tens of millions of American voters repudiating Trump’s domestic agenda and foreign policy.

Trump said this week he was willing to work with Democrats on Capitol Hill. But elevating Miller, who is known for being caustic and uncompromising, could signal a more confrontational approach and a renewed push to advance the president’s agenda on immigration and other issues, several White House officials said.

Trump had been displeased with his political and communications operations in the run-up to Tuesday’s election as his public approval ratings fell near record lows. This week, he said the White House needed to be “more aggressive” as Democrats retake congressional power, according to a person briefed on the matter.

“The mission now is more clear than ever,” Miller said on X after his appointment. “Fight with all of our soul to support our President and defend this magnificent Republic.”

Hakeem Jeffries, who is set to become the new Democratic speaker of the House, responded to the announcement by calling Miller a “reckless extremist” in a posting on X.

MILLER DRIVING IMMIGRATION CRACKDOWN

Miller, 41, is one of Trump’s longest-serving aides and one of only a few who served throughout his first and second terms in office.

Since Trump’s return to the White House in 2025, Miller has officially served as deputy chief of staff under Wiles, but he has wielded outsize influence across much of Trump’s domestic agenda and has had the president’s ear.

He is perhaps best known for driving Trump’s aggressive immigration crackdown, setting a goal of 3,000 arrests a day. The efforts to meet that target pushed masked US immigration officers into communities around the country, increasingly arresting people with no criminal records and who had been living in the country for decades.

The crackdown, however, gets poor marks with Americans. Just 36% of respondents to a Reuters/Ipsos poll completed early this week approve of it, with 54% disapproving.

Representative Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, said the party planned to investigate Miller’s immigration policies. “Stephen Miller should lawyer up,” he said.

Miller was also deeply involved in Trump’s campaign to remake the federal bureaucracy, which led to the dismissal of tens of thousands of civil servants in 2025. He was also a driving force behind the administration’s battles with universities, diversity programs and other institutions.

HAWKISH FOREIGN POLICY

On foreign policy, Miller has been a vocal supporter of Trump’s deadly military strikes on boats suspected of carrying drugs in the Caribbean and Pacific, a campaign that has raised legal questions.

He has also praised US and Israeli strikes in Iran and defended a naval blockade and sanctions as ways to weaken Tehran and curb its ability to threaten its neighbors. It is not clear whether that is still his view after voters punished Republicans this week in part for the economic fallout from the Iran war.

Marc Short, who was chief of staff to then-Vice President Mike Pence in Trump’s first term, said that in Miller, Trump is “getting someone who is wed to him” and who is willing to battle Congress over issues like immigration and congressional investigations.

“It would not suggest that there is high expectation for bipartisan legislation,” Short said in an interview.

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, who faces Democratic calls for impeachment over the Iran war, celebrated Miller’s promotion with a social media post reading, “Patriots in control,” reflecting the enthusiasm of some Trump allies for putting Miller in a position of greater authority.

SHAKE UP AFTER ELECTION SETBACK

The chief of staff typically wields great influence as the president’s gatekeeper. The person manages White House staff, organizes the president’s time and schedule, and oversees other government departments and lawmakers.

Wiles, 69, who submitted her resignation on Thursday night, will move to Trump’s political operation, according to a White House official.

The veteran political operative from Florida was the first woman to serve as White House chief of staff.

She brought decades of political experience to the role and was regarded as running a more disciplined operation than some of Trump’s prior top aides. She maintained her role even while undergoing treatment earlier this year for early-stage breast cancer.

Wiles rarely challenged Trump’s policies but brought discipline to an often chaotic operation and was seen as a voice of reason. Her exit raises questions about who will play her role.

Trump ran through four chiefs of staff – an unusually high number – during his 2017-2021 term, as they were seen to have struggled to rein in the unpredictable president.

(Reporting by Bo Erickson, Nandita Bose, Steve Holland, Jacob Bogage in Washington; Additional reporting by Bhargav Acharya and Susan Heavey; Writing by Trevor Hunnicutt; editing by Scott Malone, Colleen Jenkins, Ross Colvin and Jonathan Spicer)
